claim: Polarised mRNA transport is a prevalent mechanism for spatial control of protein synthesis.
source: Polarised mRNA transport is a prevalent mechanism for spatial control of protein synthesis.
evidence: This is a general statement about mRNA transport supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The composition of transported ribonucleoprotein particles (RNPs) and the regulation of their movement are poorly understood.
source: However, the composition of transported ribonucleoprotein particles (RNPs) and the regulation of their movement are poorly understood.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field as presented in the introduction.

claim: Microtubule minus end-directed transport of mRNAs can be reconstituted using purified components.
source: We have reconstituted microtubule minus end-directed transport of mRNAs using purified components.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through in vitro experiments.

claim: A Bicaudal-D (BicD) adaptor protein and the RNA-binding protein Egalitarian (Egl) are sufficient for long-distance mRNA transport by the dynein motor and its accessory complex dynactin.
source: A Bicaudal-D (BicD) adaptor protein and the RNA-binding protein Egalitarian (Egl) are sufficient for long-distance mRNA transport by the dynein motor and its accessory complex dynactin, thus defining a minimal transport-competent RNP.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through reconstitution experiments showing that these components alone can support transport.

claim: The minimal transport-competent RNP consists of BicD, Egl, dynein, and dynactin.
source: A Bicaudal-D (BicD) adaptor protein and the RNA-binding protein Egalitarian (Egl) are sufficient for long-distance mRNA transport by the dynein motor and its accessory complex dynactin, thus defining a minimal transport-competent RNP.
evidence: This is directly stated as a conclusion from the reconstitution experiments.

claim: RNA is required for robust activation of dynein motility.
source: Unexpectedly, the RNA is required for robust activation of dynein motility.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through comparative experiments with and without RNA.

claim: A cis-acting RNA localisation signal promotes the interaction of Egl with BicD.
source: We show that a cis-acting RNA localisation signal promotes the interaction of Egl with BicD, which licenses the latter protein to recruit dynein and dynactin.
evidence: This is demonstrated through biochemical and biophysical experiments showing enhanced Egl-BicD interaction in the presence of RNA.

claim: RNA-induced interaction of Egl with BicD licenses BicD to recruit dynein and dynactin.
source: We show that a cis-acting RNA localisation signal promotes the interaction of Egl with BicD, which licenses the latter protein to recruit dynein and dynactin.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that RNA enhances the assembly of the transport complex.

claim: BicD activation is based on RNA-induced occupancy of two Egl-binding sites on the BicD dimer.
source: Our data support a model for BicD activation based on RNA-induced occupancy of two Egl-binding sites on the BicD dimer.
evidence: This is supported by dual-labeling experiments showing two Egl molecules per BicD dimer in active transport complexes.

claim: Scaffolding of adaptor protein assemblies by cargoes is a mechanism for regulating intracellular transport.
source: Scaffolding of adaptor protein assemblies by cargoes is an attractive mechanism for regulating intracellular transport.
evidence: This is proposed as a general model based on the findings of this study.

claim: mRNA localisation contributes to diverse processes, including embryonic axis determination, epithelial polarity and neuronal plasticity.
source: By compartmentalising protein function, mRNA localisation contributes to diverse processes, including embryonic axis determination, epithelial polarity and neuronal plasticity.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field as indicated by the citations in the introduction.

claim: Trafficking of mRNAs frequently depends on the action of cytoskeletal motors, in particular those that move along the polarised microtubule network.
source: Trafficking of mRNAs frequently depends on the action of cytoskeletal motors, in particular those that move along the polarised microtubule network (Mofatteh and Bullock, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The mechanisms by which specific mRNAs are recruited to, and transported by, microtubule motors remain unclear.
source: However, the mechanisms by which specific mRNAs are recruited to, and transported by, microtubule motors remain unclear.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Microtubule-based mRNA transport operates during early development of Drosophila melanogaster.
source: One of the most tractable systems for microtubule-based mRNA transport operates during early development of Drosophila melanogaster and is responsible for localising spatial determinants of embryonic patterning to microtubule minus ends.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila system.

claim: Transport of mRNAs in Drosophila is dependent on the Egalitarian (Egl) and Bicaudal-D (BicD) proteins.
source: Transport of these mRNAs is dependent on the Egalitarian (Egl) and Bicaudal-D (BicD) proteins (Bullock and Ish-Horowicz, 2001), as well as the minus end-directed motor cytoplasmic dynein-1 (dynein) and its accessory complex dynactin (Wilkie and Davis, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genetic studies.

claim: Transport of mRNAs in Drosophila is dependent on the minus end-directed motor cytoplasmic dynein-1 (dynein) and its accessory complex dynactin.
source: Transport of these mRNAs is dependent on the Egalitarian (Egl) and Bicaudal-D (BicD) proteins (Bullock and Ish-Horowicz, 2001), as well as the minus end-directed motor cytoplasmic dynein-1 (dynein) and its accessory complex dynactin (Wilkie and Davis, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genetic studies.

claim: Egl is a 1004-amino-acid protein.
source: Egl is a 1004-amino-acid protein that directly associates with the specialised RNA stem-loops that mediate polarised transport (so-called RNA localisation signals) (Dienstbier et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a factual description of the protein supported by citation.

claim: Egl directly associates with RNA stem-loops that mediate polarised transport (RNA localisation signals).
source: Egl is a 1004-amino-acid protein that directly associates with the specialised RNA stem-loops that mediate polarised transport (so-called RNA localisation signals) (Dienstbier et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The basis of RNA recognition by Egl is not known.
source: The basis of RNA recognition by Egl is not known, although an exonuclease-like domain between residues 557 and 726 is partly responsible (Dienstbier et al., 2009).
evidence: This reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: An exonuclease-like domain between residues 557 and 726 of Egl is partly responsible for RNA recognition.
source: The basis of RNA recognition by Egl is not known, although an exonuclease-like domain between residues 557 and 726 is partly responsible (Dienstbier et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Egl uses a short N-terminal region to bind BicD.
source: Egl uses a short N-terminal region to bind BicD (Dienstbier et al., 2009), and C-terminal features to bind the LC8 dynein light chain (Navarro et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Egl uses C-terminal features to bind the LC8 dynein light chain.
source: Egl uses a short N-terminal region to bind BicD (Dienstbier et al., 2009), and C-terminal features to bind the LC8 dynein light chain (Navarro et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Mammalian BicD orthologues – BICD1 and BICD2 – associate with dynein and dynactin.
source: Mammalian BicD orthologues – BICD1 and BICD2 – associate with dynein and dynactin (Hoogenraad et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: It is not known if other factors co-operate with Egl and BicD to bridge mRNAs to the dynein transport machinery.
source: It is not known, however, if other factors co-operate with Egl and BicD to bridge mRNAs to the motor complex.
evidence: This reflects a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The isolated N-terminal region of mammalian BICD2 (BICD2N) can bridge the interaction between dynein and dynactin.
source: By forming an extended coiled-coil homodimer, the isolated N-terminal region of mammalian BICD2 (BICD2N: containing coiled-coil domain 1 (CC1) and part of CC2) can bridge the interaction between dynein and dynactin, forming a mutually dependent triple complex (Hoogenraad and Akhmanova, 2016; Splinter et al., 2012; Urnavicius et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous structural and biochemical studies.

claim: BICD2N forms an extended coiled-coil homodimer.
source: By forming an extended coiled-coil homodimer, the isolated N-terminal region of mammalian BICD2 (BICD2N: containing coiled-coil domain 1 (CC1) and part of CC2) can bridge the interaction between dynein and dynactin, forming a mutually dependent triple complex (Hoogenraad and Akhmanova, 2016; Splinter et al., 2012; Urnavicius et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The binding of dynein to BICD2N and dynactin increases the incidence of processive movement dramatically.
source: The binding of dynein to BICD2N and dynactin increases the incidence of processive movement dramatically (McKenney et al., 2014; Schlager et al., 2014), which is associated with repositioning of the dynein motor domains with respect to the microtubule (Chowdhury et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The binding of dynein to BICD2N and dynactin is associated with repositioning of the dynein motor domains with respect to the microtubule.
source: The binding of dynein to BICD2N and dynactin increases the incidence of processive movement dramatically (McKenney et al., 2014; Schlager et al., 2014), which is associated with repositioning of the dynein motor domains with respect to the microtubule (Chowdhury et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The motor moves with higher velocity once bound to BICD2N and dynactin.
source: The motor also moves with higher velocity and has increased force output once bound to BICD2N and dynactin (Belyy et al., 2016; McKenney et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The motor has increased force output once bound to BICD2N and dynactin.
source: The motor also moves with higher velocity and has increased force output once bound to BICD2N and dynactin (Belyy et al., 2016; McKenney et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The equivalent N-terminal region of Drosophila BicD stimulates dynein-based transport in vivo.
source: The equivalent N-terminal region of Drosophila BicD stimulates dynein-based transport in vivo (Dienstbier et al., 2009), indicating that this mechanism is evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The mechanism of dynein activation by BicD is evolutionarily conserved.
source: The equivalent N-terminal region of Drosophila BicD stimulates dynein-based transport in vivo (Dienstbier et al., 2009), indicating that this mechanism is evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both Drosophila and mammalian BicD proteins have similar effects.

claim: Full-length BicD proteins interact poorly with dynein and dynactin.
source: Full-length BicD proteins interact poorly with dynein and dynactin and are therefore only weak activators of dynein motility (Dienstbier et al., 2009; Hoogenraad et al., 2001, 2003; Huynh and Vale, 2017; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Full-length BicD proteins are only weak activators of dynein motility.
source: Full-length BicD proteins interact poorly with dynein and dynactin and are therefore only weak activators of dynein motility (Dienstbier et al., 2009; Hoogenraad et al., 2001, 2003; Huynh and Vale, 2017; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: BicD appears to be autoinhibited by folding back of the third coiled-coil domain (CC3) onto the dynein-activating sequences in CC1/2.
source: While mechanistic details are still lacking, BicD appears to be autoinhibited by folding back of the third coiled-coil domain (CC3) onto the dynein-activating sequences in CC1/2 (Dienstbier et al., 2009; Hoogenraad et al., 2001; Stuurman et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The interaction of CC3 with cargo-binding proteins such as Egl or Rab6 frees CC1/2 to interact with dynein and dynactin.
source: It has been proposed that the interaction of CC3 with cargo-binding proteins such as Egl or Rab6 (a G-protein that binds Golgi-derived vesicles) frees CC1/2 to interact with dynein and dynactin (Dienstbier et al., 2009; Hoogenraad and Akhmanova, 2016; Hoogenraad et al., 2001, 2003; Matanis et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a model proposed in previous studies as indicated by citations.

claim: Mutating an essential residue in the shared Rab6- and Egl-binding site in CC3 prevents Drosophila BicD from associating with dynein in vivo.
source: Consistent with this model, mutating an essential residue in the shared Rab6- and Egl-binding site in CC3 prevents Drosophila BicD from associating with dynein in vivo (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The presence of Rab6 allows full-length BICD2 to associate with dynein and dynactin and thereby activate transport in vitro.
source: It has recently been shown in vitro that the presence of Rab6 allows full-length BICD2 to associate with dynein and dynactin and thereby activate transport (Huynh and Vale, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Association of a cargo-binding protein with CC3 stimulates the assembly of an active dynein-dynactin-BicD complex.
source: This observation provides direct evidence that association of a cargo-binding protein with CC3 stimulates the assembly of an active dynein-dynactin-BicD complex, although the stoichiometry of Rab6 and BICD2 in transport complexes was not investigated.
evidence: This is inferred from the Rab6 study cited.

claim: Rab6 only associates with mammalian and Drosophila BicD proteins when it is GTP-bound (Rab6GTP).
source: Rab6 only associates with mammalian and Drosophila BicD proteins when it is GTP-bound (Rab6GTP) (Huynh and Vale, 2017; Liu et al., 2013; Matanis et al., 2002; Short et al., 2002), a state induced by association with its target membranes (Hutagalung and Novick, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Rab6GTP state is induced by association with target membranes.
source: Rab6 only associates with mammalian and Drosophila BicD proteins when it is GTP-bound (Rab6GTP) (Huynh and Vale, 2017; Liu et al., 2013; Matanis et al., 2002; Short et al., 2002), a state induced by association with its target membranes (Hutagalung and Novick, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Egl can associate with BicD CC3 in vitro in the absence of an RNA cargo.
source: Egl, on the other hand, can associate with BicD CC3 in vitro in the absence of an RNA cargo (Dienstbier et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The RNA is not involved in the relief of BicD autoinhibition by Egl (according to previous hypotheses).
source: This observation implies that the RNA is not involved in the relief of BicD autoinhibition by Egl, although this hypothesis has not been tested directly.
evidence: This is an inference from previous observations that is challenged by the current study.

claim: 80% of microtubule-associated hairy RNA puncta underwent long-distance transport in the presence of Egl/BICD2, dynein, and dynactin.
source: Gratifyingly, 80% of microtubule-associated hairy RNA puncta underwent long-distance transport (Figure 1C,D and Video 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the in vitro motility assay shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Hairy RNAs accumulated at microtubule minus ends following transport.
source: As observed previously with a Drosophila extract-based system (Soundararajan and Bullock, 2014), hairy RNAs accumulated at microtubule minus ends following transport (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A) and were also capable of diffusive motion on the microtubule lattice (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and is consistent with previous observations.

claim: Hairy RNAs were capable of diffusive motion on the microtubule lattice.
source: As observed previously with a Drosophila extract-based system (Soundararajan and Bullock, 2014), hairy RNAs accumulated at microtubule minus ends following transport (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A) and were also capable of diffusive motion on the microtubule lattice (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: I-factor RNA exhibited robust minus end-directed transport in the in vitro assay.
source: Like hairy, this RNA exhibited robust minus end-directed transport in our in vitro assay (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: No additional proteins are required for microtubule-based mRNA transport in vitro beyond Egl, BicD, dynein, and dynactin.
source: These experiments reveal that no additional proteins are required for microtubule-based mRNA transport in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the reconstitution experiments.

claim: The ILS bound to microtubules ~five times more frequently than the scrambled RNA in the presence of Egl, BICD2, dynein, and dynactin.
source: In the presence of Egl, BICD2, dynein, and dynactin, the ILS bound to microtubules ~five times more frequently than the mutant RNA and exhibited a similar relative increase in the number of processive movements (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: The ILS exhibited a similar relative increase in the number of processive movements compared to the scrambled RNA.
source: In the presence of Egl, BICD2, dynein, and dynactin, the ILS bound to microtubules ~five times more frequently than the mutant RNA and exhibited a similar relative increase in the number of processive movements (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: The transport machinery retains selectivity for RNA localisation signals in the in vitro assay.
source: These data reveal that the transport machinery retains selectivity for RNA localisation signals in our assay.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential behavior of ILS vs scrambled RNA.

claim: ~75% of the processive complexes that contained the scrambled RNA also had a signal from the ILS.
source: Further analysis revealed that ~75% of the processive complexes that contained the scrambled RNA also had a signal from the ILS (Figure 1E,H), raising the possibility that much of the transport of the mutant RNA is an indirect consequence of association with active ILS-bound transport complexes.
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Much of the transport of the mutant RNA is an indirect consequence of association with active ILS-bound transport complexes.
source: Further analysis revealed that ~75% of the processive complexes that contained the scrambled RNA also had a signal from the ILS (Figure 1E,H), raising the possibility that much of the transport of the mutant RNA is an indirect consequence of association with active ILS-bound transport complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-transport data.

claim: Egl and BICD2 were co-transported with dynein and hairy RNA in the presence of dynactin.
source: Egl and BICD2 were co-transported with dynein and hairy RNA in the presence of dynactin (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1; note that dynactin could not be labelled as it is from a native source).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The association of hairy with microtubules was barely detected when Egl/BICD2, dynactin, or dynein was excluded.
source: The association of hairy with microtubules was barely detected when Egl/BICD2, dynactin, or dynein was excluded (Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The simultaneous presence of all three protein complexes (Egl/BICD2, dynactin, and dynein) is required to link RNA to microtubules.
source: Thus, the simultaneous presence of all three protein complexes is required to link RNA to microtubules.
evidence: This is concluded from the omission experiments.

claim: In the absence of Egl/BICD2 or dynactin, dynein rarely exhibited transport but could still associate with microtubules.
source: In the absence of Egl/BICD2 or dynactin, dynein rarely exhibited transport but could still associate with microtubules (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was an ~two-fold increase in microtubule binding events when both Egl/BICD2 and dynactin were present.
source: However, there was an ~two-fold increase in microtubule binding events when both Egl/BICD2 and dynactin were present (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The combination of Egl/BICD2 and dynactin stimulates dynein's ability to associate with microtubules and move processively in the presence of RNA.
source: Thus, the combination of Egl/BICD2 and dynactin stimulates dynein's ability to associate with microtubules and move processively in the presence of RNA.
evidence: This is concluded from the binding and motility data.

claim: The number of processive movements of dynein was ~six-fold higher when the RNA was present.
source: Strikingly, the number of processive movements of dynein was ~six-fold higher when the RNA was present (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 3B.

claim: RNA increases microtubule binding by dynein in the presence of Egl/BICD2 and dynactin.
source: This reflected an increase in microtubule binding by dynein (Figure 3C), as well as the propensity for processive movement of those complexes associated with the microtubule (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: RNA increases the propensity for processive movement of dynein complexes associated with the microtubule.
source: This reflected an increase in microtubule binding by dynein (Figure 3C), as well as the propensity for processive movement of those complexes associated with the microtubule (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The mean velocity of dynein complexes bound to RNA was significantly higher than those assayed in the absence of RNA.
source: The mean velocity and run length of dynein complexes bound to RNA were also significantly higher than those assayed in the absence of RNA (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The mean run length of dynein complexes bound to RNA was significantly higher than those assayed in the absence of RNA.
source: The mean velocity and run length of dynein complexes bound to RNA were also significantly higher than those assayed in the absence of RNA (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The RNA is required for robust stimulation of dynein motility and microtubule binding in the presence of Egl/BICD2 and dynactin.
source: We conclude that the RNA is required for robust stimulation of dynein motility and microtubule binding in the presence of Egl/BICD2 and dynactin.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparative experiments with and without RNA.

claim: Hairy RNA increases the frequency of processive dynein movements when dynactin and a complex of Egl bound to Drosophila BicD (DmBicD) is included in the assay.
source: The hairy RNA significantly increased the number of processive movements of dynein in the presence of dynactin and Egl/DmBicD (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: RNA enhances microtubule binding of the motor in the presence of Egl/DmBicD and dynactin.
source: This effect was again associated with enhanced microtubule binding of the motor, as well as increased probability of processive movement after engaging with the microtubule (Figure 3I,J).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3I.

claim: RNA increases the probability of processive movement after dynein engages with the microtubule in the presence of Egl/DmBicD and dynactin.
source: This effect was again associated with enhanced microtubule binding of the motor, as well as increased probability of processive movement after engaging with the microtubule (Figure 3I,J).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3J.

claim: RNA enhances the mean velocity of dynein movements in the presence of Egl/DmBicD and dynactin.
source: As was observed in the experiments with Egl/BICD2, the RNA also enhanced the mean velocity and length of dynein movements (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNA enhances the mean length of dynein movements in the presence of Egl/DmBicD and dynactin.
source: As was observed in the experiments with Egl/BICD2, the RNA also enhanced the mean velocity and length of dynein movements (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNA gates the activation of dynein motility by a co-evolved Egl/BicD complex.
source: Thus, RNA also gates the activation of dynein motility by a co-evolved Egl/BicD complex.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments with Egl/DmBicD.

claim: The frequency of co-localisation of Egl with microtubule-bound dynein increased by ~six-fold when the RNA was present.
source: Although there was some association of dynein with Egl in the absence of RNA, the frequency of co-localisation increased by ~six-fold when the RNA was present (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 4C.

claim: RNA stimulates the association of BICD2 with microtubule-associated dynein.
source: We confirmed that the RNA also stimulates the association of BICD2 with microtubule-associated dynein by labelling BICD2 within the purified Egl/BICD2 complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Many of the dynein complexes bound to Egl/BICD2 were motile regardless of whether RNA was present or absent.
source: Many of the dynein complexes bound to Egl/BICD2 were motile (regardless of whether RNA was present of absent) (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), indicating that they were also complexed with dynactin (McKenney et al., 2014; Schlager et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ability of RNA to activate processive dynein motion is associated with enhanced assembly of the Egl/BICD2/dynein/dynactin complex.
source: Thus, the ability of RNA to activate processive dynein motion is associated with enhanced assembly of the Egl/BICD2/dynein/dynactin complex.
evidence: This is concluded from the co-localization experiments.

claim: The addition of hairy RNA led to detectable co-precipitation of p150 and Dhc with Egl::GFP from Drosophila embryo extracts.
source: p150 and Dhc were not detected in the Egl::GFP immunoprecipitate in the absence of exogenous RNA, indicating that the association of Egl with dynein and dynactin is of low affinity or low abundance. In contrast, the addition of the hairy RNA led to detectable co-precipitation of the dynein and dynactin components with Egl::GFP.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: Assembly of the transport complex is promoted by the RNA in the context of both purified and endogenously-expressed proteins.
source: Thus, assembly of the transport complex is promoted by the RNA in the context of both purified and endogenously-expressed proteins.
evidence: This is concluded from both the in vitro and immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: The Egldlc2pt/BICD2 complex supported robust transport of hairy RNA in the presence of dynein and dynactin.
source: The Egldlc2pt/BICD2 complex supported robust transport of hairy RNA in the presence of dynein and dynactin (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The mutant Egl/BICD2 complex (Egldlc2pt) still supported the RNA-induced increase in processive movement of dynein.
source: Moreover, the mutant Egl/BICD2 complex still supported the RNA-induced increase in processive movement and microtubule binding of dynein in the presence of dynactin (Figure 5C–E), as well as higher mean velocities and run lengths of the motor (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: The mutant Egl/BICD2 complex (Egldlc2pt) still supported the RNA-induced increase in microtubule binding of dynein.
source: Moreover, the mutant Egl/BICD2 complex still supported the RNA-induced increase in processive movement and microtubule binding of dynein in the presence of dynactin (Figure 5C–E), as well as higher mean velocities and run lengths of the motor (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: The interaction of Egl with LC8 does not play a significant role in activation of dynein by RNA.
source: Thus, the interaction of Egl with LC8 does not play a significant role in activation of dynein by RNA.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments with the Egldlc2pt mutant.

claim: The ILS caused a large change in the elution profile of the Egl/BICD2 complex compared to the RNA-free form.
source: We first mixed the 59-nt ILS RNA with purified Egl/BICD2 and performed size exclusion chromatography. The RNA localisation signal caused a large change in the elution profile of the protein complex compared to the RNA-free form (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating a substantial increase in molar mass or a conformational change.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presence of the ILS caused a large increase in mean molar mass of Egl/BICD2 compared to RNA-free samples.
source: Over a range of protein concentrations, the presence of the ILS caused a large increase in mean molar mass compared to RNA-free samples (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: SEC-MALS confirmed that the ILS substantially increases the mean molar mass of the Egl/BICD2 sample.
source: An orthogonal method for determining molar masses – size-exclusion chromatography with multi-angle light scattering (SEC-MALS) – confirmed that the ILS substantially increases the mean molar mass of the Egl/BICD2 sample (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The scrambled ILS RNA elicited a relatively small increase in mean molar mass of Egl/BICD2.
source: Despite being present in a 10-fold molar access to Egl/BICD2, the scrambled ILS RNA elicited a relatively small increase in mean molar mass (Figure 6C), confirming selectivity of the Egl/BICD2 complex for an active RNA localisation signal.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The Egl/BICD2 complex shows selectivity for an active RNA localisation signal.
source: Despite being present in a 10-fold molar access to Egl/BICD2, the scrambled ILS RNA elicited a relatively small increase in mean molar mass (Figure 6C), confirming selectivity of the Egl/BICD2 complex for an active RNA localisation signal.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential effects of ILS vs scrambled RNA.

claim: The ILS-induced increases in mass were associated with enhanced interaction of BICD2 and Egl.
source: Analysis of peak SEC-MALS fractions by SDS-PAGE revealed that the ILS-induced increases in mass were associated with enhanced interaction of BICD2 and Egl (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The mean molar mass of the Egl/DmBicD complex increased substantially in the presence of the ILS.
source: We also used SEC-MALS to determine the effect of the ILS on the purified complex of Egl and DmBicD. The mean molar mass of the peak fractions increased substantially in the presence of the ILS, and this was again associated with increased binding of Egl and the BicD protein (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: The Egl/BICD2 and Egl/DmBicD complexes readily equilibrate with constituent species and this is counteracted by the RNA localisation signal.
source: Collectively, these experiments reveal that the Egl/BICD2 and Egl/DmBicD complexes readily equilibrate with constituent species and that this is counteracted by the RNA localisation signal.
evidence: This is concluded from the SE-AUC and SEC-MALS experiments.

claim: BICD2 is a dimer.
source: It was previously shown that DmBicD is a dimer (Stuurman et al., 1999), and we confirmed that this is also the case for BICD2 using SEC-MALS (Figure 6B; observed molar mass 186.7 ± 0.5 kDa).
evidence: This is confirmed by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 39% of the motile complexes with a BICD2 signal were labelled with both TMR and Alexa647 dyes.
source: When the labelled Egl/SNAP::BICD2 sample was used in motility assays with dynein, dynactin and hairy RNA, 39% of the motile complexes with a BICD2 signal were labelled with both dyes (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The co-localisation analysis fits well with there being a single BICD2 dimer in transport complexes.
source: Our co-localisation analysis therefore fits well with there being a single BICD2 dimer in transport complexes (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is concluded from the dual-labeling experiments and statistical analysis.

claim: 37% of fluorescent Egl complexes were dual-labelled in the presence of RNA.
source: When the procedure was repeated with SNAP-tagged Egl co-expressed with BICD2, the proportion of fluorescent complexes that was dual-labelled in the presence of RNA was 37% (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 7E.

claim: There are two Egl molecules in the vast majority of active RNA transport complexes.
source: Correcting for the small fraction of Egl::SNAP molecules that are unlabelled, this result indicates that there are two Egl molecules in the vast majority of active RNA transport complexes (Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This is concluded from the dual-labeling experiments and statistical analysis.

claim: Even when the assembly of the transport machinery is inefficient, motility is usually associated with the presence of two Egl molecules in a complex.
source: When this experiment was performed in the absence of RNA, the relatively small number of motile Egl complexes observed also had signal from both dyes in 41% of cases (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). These data indicate that even when the assembly of the transport machinery is inefficient, motility is usually associated with the presence of two Egl molecules in a complex.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: 14% of labelled motile RNPs had signal from both Cy3 and Cy5 dyes.
source: Of the labelled motile RNPs, 14% had signal from both dyes (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 7G.

claim: 30% of RNPs contained two RNAs and 70% contained one RNA.
source: Considering that the same proportion of complexes should have two Cy3 dyes or two Cy5 dyes, and that the labelling efficiency means that a small fraction of RNA molecules will contain neither dye, these data indicate that 30% of RNPs contained two RNAs and 70% contained one RNA (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is calculated from the dual-labeling data.

claim: Transported hairy RNPs assembled in Drosophila extracts exclusively contain a single RNA.
source: We previously found that transported hairy RNPs assembled in Drosophila extracts exclusively contain a single RNA (Amrute-Nayak and Bullock, 2012; Soundararajan and Bullock, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The vast majority of BicD dimers in active transport complexes associate with two Egl polypeptides.
source: In summary, the results of the dual-labelling experiments are consistent with the vast majority of BicD dimers in active transport complexes associating with two Egl polypeptides, and most associating with a single RNA.
evidence: This is concluded from the dual-labeling experiments.

claim: Most BicD dimers in active transport complexes associate with a single RNA.
source: In summary, the results of the dual-labelling experiments are consistent with the vast majority of BicD dimers in active transport complexes associating with two Egl polypeptides, and most associating with a single RNA.
evidence: This is concluded from the dual-labeling experiments.

claim: The RNA localisation signal licenses BicD to bind dynein and dynactin by facilitating the association of BicD CC3 with two Egl molecules.
source: Together with our earlier results, these data support a model in which the RNA localisation signal licenses BicD to bind dynein and dynactin by facilitating the association of BicD CC3 with two Egl molecules (see below).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the collective data from the study.

claim: No other factors appear to be obligatory for linkage of the RNA to dynein beyond Egl, BicD, dynein, and dynactin.
source: Although genetic experiments indicate that other proteins can modulate the mRNA transport process in vivo (Dix et al., 2013; Hain et al., 2014), no other factors appear to be obligatory for linkage of the RNA to dynein.
evidence: This is concluded from the reconstitution experiments.

claim: A purified Egl/BicD complex does not efficiently associate with dynein and dynactin in the absence of an RNA localisation signal.
source: Previous observations suggested that binding of a cargo-associated protein such as Egl to the C-terminal region of BicD is sufficient to overcome the autoinhibited state of the full-length protein, and thereby lead to recruitment of dynein and dynactin. Our study reveals that a purified Egl/BicD complex does not efficiently associate with dynein and dynactin in the absence of an RNA localisation signal.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study.

claim: The availability of the cargo gates robust activation of dynein motility.
source: Thus, the availability of the cargo gates robust activation of dynein motility.
evidence: This is concluded from the RNA-dependence of dynein activation.

claim: The previously reported interaction of Egl with LC8 is not required for RNA-directed activation of dynein motility.
source: We show that the previously reported interaction of Egl with LC8 (Navarro et al., 2004) is not required for RNA-directed activation of dynein motility.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with the Egldlc2pt mutant.

claim: A key consequence of RNA binding to Egl is stimulation of the interaction of BicD with dynein and dynactin.
source: Our data indicate that a key consequence of RNA binding to Egl is stimulation of the interaction of BicD with dynein and dynactin.
evidence: This is concluded from the co-localization and biochemical experiments.

claim: RNA-bound Egl must overcome the autoinhibition of full-length BicD that prevents CC1/2 from engaging with dynein and dynactin.
source: Thus, RNA-bound Egl must overcome the autoinhibition of full-length BicD that prevents CC1/2 from engaging with dynein and dynactin.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing RNA-dependent activation.

claim: A folded back conformation of full-length DmBicD was retained in the presence of Egl alone, but not detected in the presence of both RNA and Egl.
source: Negative stain electron microscopy in a contemporary study (Sladewski et al., 2018) lends further support to this notion; a folded back conformation of full-length DmBicD (Stuurman et al., 1999), which is likely to represent the autoinhibited state (Hoogenraad et al., 2001, 2003; Liu et al., 2013), was retained in the presence of Egl alone, but not detected in the presence of both RNA and Egl.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a contemporary study.

claim: The recruitment of RNA to dynein by Egl/BICD2 is dependent on dynactin.
source: The recruitment of RNA to dynein by Egl/BICD2 is dependent on dynactin (Figure 2B,C), as is also the case for the interaction of BICD2N with the motor complex (McKenney et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B,C and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: The ability of RNA-bound Egl/BICD2 to augment dynein's binding to microtubules is shared with BICD2N.
source: Furthermore, the ability of RNA-bound Egl/BICD2 to augment dynein's binding to microtubules (Figure 3C), as well as its velocity (Figure 3E) and run length (Figure 3F), is also shared with BICD2N (McKenney et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in the figures and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: A single BICD2N dimer and a single dynactin can recruit one or two dynein complexes.
source: Very recently, it has been shown that a single BICD2N dimer and a single dynactin can recruit one or two dynein complexes (Grotjahn et al., 2018; Urnavicius et al., 2018), with the binding of the second motor increasing velocity and run length (Urnavicius et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Two dynein motors are present in the majority of transport RNPs.
source: Sladewski et al., 2018 provide evidence that two dynein motors are present in the majority of their transport RNPs, raising the possibility that interaction of RNA-bound Egl with BICD2 modulates the velocity and run length of transport complexes by favouring the two-motor-binding conformation of CC1.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a contemporary study.

claim: An in vitro study of a yeast actin-based mRNA transport complex reported stimulation of processive movement by the RNA cargo.
source: An in vitro study of a yeast actin-based mRNA transport complex also reported stimulation of processive movement by the RNA cargo (Sladewski et al., 2013) (although an independent investigation of the same complex reported no influence of the RNA [Heym et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The mechanism proposed for RNA-mediated activation of dynein is distinct from the one proposed for the yeast actin-based transport complex.
source: The mechanism that we and Sladewski et al., 2018 propose for RNA-mediated activation of dynein – involving relief of autoinhibition of an adaptor – is distinct from the one proposed for the yeast transport complex, which is based on RNA-dependent dimerisation of monomers of the myosin motor (Sladewski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison of mechanisms based on the current study and previous work.

claim: Multiple strategies may have evolved to co-ordinate the processivity of cytoskeletal motors with the availability of an RNA cargo.
source: Thus, multiple strategies may have evolved to co-ordinate the processivity of cytoskeletal motors with the availability of an RNA cargo.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the comparison of different systems.

claim: The most parsimonious explanation for the data is that the RNA localisation signal promotes the occupancy of CC3 with Egl, thereby freeing CC1/2 to interact with dynein and dynactin.
source: Although we cannot rule out additional mechanisms of RNA-mediated activation of BicD, the most parsimonious explanation for our data is that the RNA localisation signal promotes the occupancy of CC3 with Egl, thereby freeing CC1/2 to interact with dynein and dynactin (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the collective data, illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: Occupancy of both Egl-binding sites of BicD CC3 favours the relief of BicD autoinhibition and recruitment of dynein and dynactin.
source: It is striking that the vast majority of active transport complexes contain two Egl polypeptides per BicD dimer, even when the transport process is compromised by the omission of RNA. This finding suggests that occupancy of both Egl-binding sites of BicD CC3 favours the relief of BicD autoinhibition and recruitment of dynein and dynactin.
evidence: This is inferred from the stoichiometry data.

claim: Free Egl is monomeric.
source: Our SEC-MALS analysis indicates that free Egl is monomeric (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: BicD proteins are implicated in transport of a diverse range of cellular cargoes and pathogens by dynein and dynactin.
source: In addition to Rab6GTP-associated vesicles and Egl-associated mRNAs, BicD proteins are implicated in transport of a diverse range of cellular cargoes and pathogens by dynein and dynactin (Dharan et al., 2017; Hoogenraad and Akhmanova, 2016; Indran et al., 2010; Redwine et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: BicD CC3 can simultaneously bind two Rab6GTP proteins.
source: The finding that BicD CC3 can simultaneously bind two Rab6GTP proteins (Liu et al., 2013) is compatible with this scenario.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The Drosophila sequence of the Egl/Rab6GTP-binding site has 71% identity and 93% similarity with the mouse and human sequence.
source: The Drosophila sequence has 71% identity and 93% similarity with the mouse and human sequence.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The amount of soluble Egl is greatly increased by co-expression of BICD2.
source: The amount of soluble Egl is greatly increased by co-expression of BICD2.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The yield of Egl was extremely low in the absence of BICD2 co-expression.
source: The yield of Egl was extremely low in the absence of BICD2 co-expression, presumably due to on-going solubility issues.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The ratio of absorbance values at 260 to 280 nm for the peak fractions of Egl/BICD2 indicates that there was little, if any, RNA co-purified from the insect cells.
source: The ratio of absorbance values at 260 to 280 nm for the peak fractions indicates that there was little, if any, RNA co-purified from the insect cells (A260:A280 is 0.57 for pure protein and 1.05 for a sample with 95% protein and 5% nucleic acid [Glasel, 1995]).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and is based on spectrophotometric analysis.
